summary: Describes a preemption priority policy element for signaled policy-based admission protocols such as RSVP and COPS, which lets important reservations bump less important ones. It is a standards-track document, and it was replaced by RFC 3181.

eli5.summary: Like a VIP line, it lets important requests take the spot of less important ones when space runs out.

questions: when can a flow preempt another
subtitle: Let important network reservations bump less important ones when space runs out.

tldr.problem: Networks often have more requests for resources than available capacity. Administrators want to prioritize important traffic, but admission decisions are typically made in order of arrival.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a preemption priority policy element for signaled admission protocols like RSVP and COPS. Each flow gets a preemption priority (how forcefully it claims resources) and a defending priority (how hard it resists preemption once admitted). Higher-priority new flows can kick out lower-priority existing flows to make room.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can set policies so critical reservations are never rejected just because less important ones arrived first. The protocol was updated by RFC 3181.

facts.label: Merge strategies
facts.value: 3 (highest QoS, highest priority, or error on heterogeneous)

today: RFC 2751 is a standards-track Internet Standard defining preemption priority for signaled policy-based admission control. It was updated by RFC 3181, which clarified and extended the mechanism.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Traditional admission control systems accept traffic reservations in order of arrival until capacity is exhausted. But networks need smarter policies. This RFC defines a preemption priority policy element for signaled admission protocols like RSVP (used for quality-of-service reservations) and COPS (a protocol for policy control). The element lets a network node choose which flows to admit by importance, not arrival time, and even bump previously admitted low-priority flows to make room for high-priority new ones.

Each flow declares two priority numbers: a preemption priority (how aggressively it can preempt others) and a defending priority (how hard it resists preemption after admission). A large gap between the two provides stability: once a flow is admitted with high defending priority, it is unlikely to be preempted.
sections.eli5: Imagine a concert hall with reserved seats. Normally, reservations are honored in order. But with preemption priority, a VIP who books late can bump a regular ticket-holder if the hall is full.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
The policy element sits at the network node where a decision is needed. A Policy Decision Point (PDP, a management component) creates the element and sends it to network edges. Along the way, Local Decision Points (LDPs, less intelligent nodes) can forward, merge, or simplify the elements without changing the intent. Policy Enforcement Points (PEPs, the actual routers) use the priorities to decide which flows to admit and which to preempt.

The element is stateless: it carries all information needed to make a decision without any history or external data. This keeps the protocol simple and fast. In the format, a 12-byte field carries: a preemption priority (16-bit, higher is more aggressive), a defending priority (16-bit, higher means harder to preempt), a merge strategy (how to combine priorities when flows combine), and error codes (what went wrong if the element was rejected).
sections.eli5: A manager at the concert hall writes on a ticket: "This customer has priority 8 to book a seat (can kick out priority 3), and once seated, requires priority 6 to be booted." The ticket is passed to ticket sellers and staff; they follow the rules without asking the manager each time.

sections.title: Merging Priorities and Errors
sections.content:
When multiple flows merge at a node, their priorities must be combined. The RFC defines three merge strategies. Take priority of highest QoS (recommended) uses the priority of whichever flow has the most demanding quality needs. This prevents lower-QoS flows from freeloading on high priorities. Take highest priority is simpler but risky: a low-QoS flow with high priority can unfairly preempt. Force error on heterogeneous merge is the safest for controlled networks: mixed-QoS flows are rejected rather than merged.

When errors occur (a flow is preempted or heterogeneity is detected), the node sends the preempting or offending PREEMPTION_PRI element back toward the policy decision point that originated the affected flow. That PDP can then raise the priority and resubmit, or decide differently.
sections.eli5: If two reserved-seat requests merge into one, which priority wins? The RFC says use the priority of the customer who has the fanciest seat requirements. Or simpler: just reject the merge if they do not match. The hall tells the original bookers why the request was bumped or rejected.

sections.title: Security and Scope
sections.content:
The RFC requires that preemption priority elements be protected by the RSVP or COPS integrity mechanisms (cryptographic signatures or other integrity checks). The protocol itself is intended for trusted networks or single administrative domains; no new security is added because preemption priority already sits within the security envelope of its carrier protocol.

The design is deliberately simple and lightweight. Nodes can implement the policy element locally without external policy servers, making it suitable for routers and network equipment where every cycle counts. The element is stateless, meaning a node can apply it without remembering previous flows or consulting external databases.
sections.eli5: Trust the ticket. If your manager signed it, it is genuine. Do not add extra locks on top. The protocol is simple so that busy computers can apply it fast.
